result.summary: The Danaids fear the approaching ships of Aegyptus' sons, and Danaüs goes to fetch help. The Egyptian Herald seizes the maidens, but the Argive King arrives, refuses to surrender them, and offers them shelter in the city.

scenes.title: Fear as the ships approach
scenes.summary: The Chorus panic as the Egyptian ships near; Danaüs reassures them and leaves to seek help.
scenes.stakes: The maidens risk being seized and forced into marriage with their cousins.

scenes.title: The maidens' despairing lament
scenes.summary: Left alone, the Chorus wish for death or escape rather than marriage and pray to Zeus.
scenes.stakes: Forced marriage, which they would rather escape by death.

scenes.title: The Herald seizes the maidens
scenes.summary: The Herald threatens and drags the Chorus toward the ships while they cry for help.
scenes.stakes: The maidens face violent abduction and forced marriage.

scenes.title: The King confronts the Herald
scenes.summary: The King rebukes the Herald, declares the people's decree not to surrender the women, sends him off, and offers the maidens lodging.
scenes.stakes: Argos risks war with Aegyptus' sons by protecting the suppliants.

alias_notes.explanation: The stage direction identifies him as envoy of Aegyptus' sons.

notable_quotes.reason: The King stresses that the decision comes from free, spoken popular will, not written law.
The maidens prefer death to forced marriage.

analysis.text: The passage dramatizes the conflict between violent compulsion and the sanctity of suppliants, with the maidens' consent in marriage at its heart.
The King's appeal to a unanimous vote of the people reflects Athenian democratic ideals projected onto mythical Argos.

fun_facts.text: The play is often thought to be among Aeschylus' earliest surviving works and gives the chorus the leading role.

language_notes.text: "Adread" is an archaic form meaning afraid, in the same pattern as "afire" or "ashore".
"Fordone" is archaic for utterly exhausted or overcome.
Arms "well seasoned by the noonday heat" means soldiers hardened by sun and labour, answering the Egyptians' fearsome numbers.
"Recking naught of" means paying no heed to; they respect altars no more than scavenging birds do.
"Yon tridents" refers to emblems of Poseidon, the sea god, set up at the shore as sacred symbols of the place.
The proverb says wolves overpower dogs; byblus (papyrus) fruit, Egyptian, cannot rival wheat, the grain of Argos. The Argives are the stronger.
"Shepherds of ships" is a poetic way of saying sailors or captains.
"Apian land" is an old name for Argos, the Peloponnese region where the Danaids have sought refuge.
"The look-out my father held" refers to Danaus watching from a height and sighting the pursuing ships of Aegyptus' sons, which began their ruin.
"Halter-noose" means a hanging rope; the maiden prefers suicide by hanging to marriage.
"Beetling" describes a crag overhanging or jutting out menacingly.
The "males of the race of Aegyptus" are the fifty sons of Aegyptus, cousins whom the Danaids flee rather than marry.
The "beam of the balance" evokes Zeus weighing human fates, as in Homeric scales; he decides outcomes.
Goads are sharp pointed sticks used to drive cattle; the Herald treats the maidens like livestock.
"Murrain" is an old word for a deadly cattle plague, used here as a curse.
The "cattle-nurturing stream" is the Nile, whose flooding feeds Egypt; the maidens swear never to see their homeland river again if taken.
Sarpedon's sandy barrow is a headland, probably on the Thracian coast; the maidens wish the Herald's ship wrecked by winds there.
"Haling" means dragging or hauling by force.
Zeus is called "son of Earth" as an appeal to the local land's own Zeus, here invoked with Mother Earth.
Aegyptus' sons are the maidens' cousins, whom they are fleeing; the Herald means they will find masters, not refuge.
"Sirrah" is an old contemptuous form of address to an inferior, here used to scold the Herald.
Pelasgian is the name this translation gives to the people of the King's realm, Argos; the King is Pelasgus.
"Barbarian" here means a non-Greek foreigner, not a savage. "Waxest" means growest; the King mocks the Herald's arrogance.
The King says the Herald's wits have many misses and no hits: he is entirely wrong in his conduct.
Hermes, god of heralds and travellers, is called Searcher; the Herald claims he announced himself to Hermes as protector of messengers.
"Despoilers of the gods" refers to the Herald's seizure of women who have taken refuge at the gods' altars.
"I trow" means I believe. The Herald says war is decided by battle, not by witnesses or silver payment.
The decree is compared to a rivet driven clean through, meaning it is fixed and cannot be undone.
The King says the decision is not written on tablets or sealed scrolls but spoken openly by free men.
"Barley-bree" means beer; the King says the Argives are real men, not weak drinkers of Egyptian beer.

context_notes.text: The Argive assembly had just voted to protect the Danaïds, the fifty daughters of Danaüs, who fled forced marriage to their cousins.
Aegyptus was Danaüs's brother; his fifty sons pursue the Danaïds to compel them into marriage.
Danaüs goes to the city to bring Argive help, leaving the Chorus at the altars.
Hades is the god of the dead and ruler of the underworld; the maiden imagines him as a preferable husband.
Zeus protected suppliants, those who sought sanctuary, so the Chorus appeal to his sacred duty.
The Herald serves the sons of Aegyptus, who want to force the Danaids, daughters of Danaus, into marriage. The maidens have taken sanctuary at Argos.
The Herald sneers that the maidens, as foreign suppliants, have no city to protect them and no standing.
The Herald denies the Argive gods any claim on him, dismissing the sanctuary's protection of suppliants.
The Egyptian gods are those of the Nile, the homeland of Aegyptus' sons, who are pursuing their cousins the Danaids.
Aegyptus' sons are the fifty cousins whom the fifty daughters of Danaus have fled to avoid marrying.
The King refers to a vote of the Argive assembly, an important feature of the play's portrayal of democratic decision-making.

literary_notes.text: The ships are given swift "wings", conveying their speed and the pursuers' menace.
Calling the Egyptians "shameless dogs" dehumanizes them and stresses their impiety and lust.
Danaüs turns the dog image into a proverb of wolves, wheat and papyrus, contrasting Argive and Egyptian strength.
Night is shown as breeding anxiety in the pilot, heightening the sense of looming danger.
Comparing themselves to smoke and "viewless dust" conveys their wish to become insubstantial and vanish.
Death is called a "lord and master", turning the marriage language bitterly against itself: Hades is preferred to a husband.
The vivid, desolate crag with snow clouds and vultures mirrors the maidens' inner desolation and extremity.
The Chorus turn from their own despair to address the gods and Zeus directly, as if present.
Calling the Herald a crocodile ties him to Egypt and paints him as a savage, predatory beast.
Comparing the Herald to a spider slowly dragging them away conveys creeping, inescapable menace and the maidens' helplessness.
The viper image continues the maidens' portrayal of their pursuer as a venomous animal, not a man.
The Herald's comfort is bitterly ironic: the 'kings' he promises are the hated suitors, so reassurance is really a threat.
Misses against hits sets the Herald's many errors beside his zero successes, a sharp, mocking contrast.
The decree is likened to a rivet hammered into place, expressing its firmness and permanence.
Unwritten, spoken law is set against written tablets, stressing the King's personal, open authority.
The King turns the Herald's wish for victory to "the men" back on him, claiming that the Argives are the true men.
